## The idea

The top bass-staff line represents A3, while the bottom treble line represents
E4. Middle C lies in the space between the two staves and can be written on a
short ledger line approached from either direction. Rather than separate pitch
systems for the two clefs, the grand staff presents two windows onto one
continuous coordinate space.

The *bass clef* anchors F3 on the second line from the top. In the middle-C
coordinates introduced in Lesson 38, the bottom bass line G2 is `-10` and the
top line A3 is `-2`. A *grand staff* aligns bass and treble so low and high
voices share a timeline. Changing clef changes which span is convenient to
display; it does not change the pitch arithmetic underneath.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 84

letters = [:c, :d, :e, :f, :g, :a, :b]
semitones = {c: 0, d: 2, e: 4, f: 5, g: 7, a: 9, b: 11}

define :staff_midi do |position, letters, semitones|
  letter = letters[position % 7]
  octave = 4 + (position / 7).floor
  12 * (octave + 1) + semitones[letter]
end

define :play_events do |events, synth_name|
  use_synth synth_name
  cursor = 0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    play event[:note], release: event[:duration] * 0.85,
      amp: event.fetch(:amp, 0.7)
    sleep event[:duration]
    cursor = event[:start] + event[:duration]
  end
end

bass_positions = [-10, -8, -6, -5, -7, -9, -10, -7]
melody_positions = [2, 4, 5, 7, 6, 5, 4, 2]

bass = bass_positions.each_with_index.map do |position, index|
  {note: staff_midi(position, letters, semitones), start: index * 2,
   duration: 2, amp: 0.55}
end
melody = melody_positions.each_with_index.map do |position, index|
  {note: staff_midi(position, letters, semitones), start: index * 2,
   duration: 2, amp: 0.75}
end

in_thread { play_events bass, :fm }
play_events melody, :piano
```

The two voices cover the same sixteen beats in different registers. Their event
records share one schema, and the concurrent renderers start against the same
clock. Because staff positions remain visible until conversion, you can enter
the low and high staves from the page first and inspect the resulting MIDI values
as a later, separate step.

## Change one thing

1. Add seven to every bass position. Each note rises by one diatonic octave and
   keeps its letter name, but the low voice now presses into the melody's range.
   Listen for loss of separation without mistaking it for a pitch-decoding error.
2. Exchange the two synths. Register remains unchanged, yet timbre redistributes
   attention between the voices. This distinguishes what the clef encodes from
   what the renderer contributes.
3. Give both voices a coordinate-zero middle C on the final beat. They resolve
   to the same MIDI number, demonstrating that middle C belongs to the shared
   system rather than to either clef alone.

## Why it works

Both clefs call `staff_midi` because position zero has been defined for the
whole pitch space. Reading bass is still a matter of measuring a diatonic offset
from middle C, exactly as in treble. A clef-specific function could begin from
its own anchor, but after applying the correct offset it would reach the same
global coordinate.

The grand staff also suggests a concurrency model. Bass and melody remain
independent event arrays while sharing one clock. `in_thread` starts the low
renderer as the main thread begins the high one. Common start times keep vertical
alignments intact; separate arrays allow one voice to be corrected without
shifting events in the other.

Keyboard scores often associate bass clef with the left hand and treble with the
right, but clef and hand are different concepts. Hands cross, and instruments
other than keyboards read both clefs. Naming the arrays by musical range avoids
embedding a performance convention in the decoded score.

Absolute starts make vertical alignment testable. Events with the same `:start`
sound together even when their note heads occupy different staves. Barlines give
the voices common metric checkpoints. Before playback, compare the final start
plus duration for both arrays; unequal totals should be explained by the source,
not discovered later as apparent thread drift.

## Take it further

Encode eight bars of two-voice music from a printed grand staff. Preserve each
original staff coordinate beside `:note`, `:start`, and `:duration`, and assert
that the two voices reach the same final beat. Include a ledger-line note in
each clef and one middle C shared between them. Render the lines with contrasting
synths, then use the stored coordinates to trace any doubtful pitch back to its
place on the page.
